evidence: pydivsufsort sa_search(text,sa,pattern) returns (count, first SA row), so contains/count/locate; text is the input. int64 SA path above 2^31. suffix-trees find/find_all are the tree route.
Literal patterns only: suffix-trees find/find_all and pydivsufsort sa_search take plain str/bytes/int arrays. No wildcard, IUPAC or character-class matching in README or code.
No approximate index search. pydivsufsort levenshtein() is pairwise DP. suffix-trees nodes (root, transition_links, depth, idx) are reachable, so backtracking would be user code.
pydivsufsort common_substrings(s1,s2,limit) lists maximal common substring pairs (idx1,idx2,len), tested vs brute force. Two texts only, Python-list output, no MUM filter, pair blow-up on repeats.
No matching-statistics or streaming-anchor API. suffix-trees offers find/find_all/lcs/lcsm; pydivsufsort offers SA/LCP/BWT/LZ helpers and kmp_censor_stream (KMP, not MS).
suffix-trees STree(list of str/bytes) builds a generalized suffix tree; lcs()/lcsm() over all or selected strings. No k-common or document listing/counting; pure Python, toy-scale.
No reverse-complement support in either package; a user must append the reverse-complement text before indexing.
suffix-trees nodes expose parent, transition_links, depth, idx, is_leaf() (suffix links underscore-private, undocumented). pydivsufsort lcp_segtree/lcp_query give LCP of suffix pairs.
pydivsufsort: most_frequent_substrings, repeated_substrings (LCP-interval repeats), Lempel-Ziv complexity, LPF. suffix-trees: lcs/lcsm. No LRS, distinct-substring count or supermaximal API.
pydivsufsort wraps libdivsufsort: published 0.546 s for E.coli 4.64 MB (8.5 MB/s, 2008 Core2). No head-to-head vs libsais. suffix-trees is pure-Python McCreight (class ~1e5 bp/s).
libdivsufsort documents 5n+O(1) bytes (int32 SA + text); int64 SA above 2^31-1 chars. suffix-trees keeps a Python object per node (est. hundreds of bytes/char, not measured).
sa_search = binary search over SA, O(m log n); no published latency. Unpublished local run: ~6-8 us per 20-mer on 100 Mbp random DNA incl. ctypes call. suffix-trees find() is pure Python.
README: divsufsort64 (int64) chosen automatically when n >= 2^31-1; sa_search64 exists. No documented run at 3 Gbp (would need ~27 GB RAM).
No external-memory mode; build needs all data in RAM. SA is a plain numpy array, so np.save + memmap for queries is a user workaround (unverified).
README: wheels built with OpenMP (OMP_NUM_THREADS). Unpublished local test, 50 Mbp: 1/2/4 threads = 4.10/3.48/3.30 s (1.24x at 4). No documented near-linear speed-up.
No thread-safety statement. Query paths (sa_search, find) are read-only and ctypes calls release the GIL, but concurrent use is neither documented nor tested.
suffix-trees online=True: Ukkonen append(), queryable between appends; find() exact, find_all() may miss suffix occurrences (documented caveat). No delete/insert of texts; pydivsufsort is static.
No compressed index. pydivsufsort bw_transform/inverse_bw_transform expose the BWT, but occ/rank structure and SA sampling for an FM-index would be user code.
pydivsufsort accepts str/bytes and any int dtype (int8..uint64) by re-encoding, slower than uint8; suffix-trees takes any str/bytes. No 2-bit or sigma=4 optimised path.
No persistence API. pydivsufsort returns numpy arrays (user np.save/np.load); suffix-trees is a Python object graph with no serializer. No format spec, versioning or checksum.
Best .NET route: P/Invoke the C-ABI libdivsufsort / libdivsufsort64 shared libs bundled in the pydivsufsort wheel (loaded via ctypes in dll.py). suffix-trees is pure Python with no .NET route.
PyPI only: suffix-trees 0.4.0; pydivsufsort 0.0.20 with prebuilt Linux/macOS/Windows wheels (incl. arm64). No CLI or server surface; a conda packaging request (issue #54) is open.
pydivsufsort: pytest vs naive reference SA/BWT/LCP/common-substring, CI on 3 OS x Py3.9/3.12 + codecov. suffix-trees: pytest + hypothesis, vectors vs str.find, CI on Py3.9-3.14.
MIT both. suffix-trees 0.4.0 released 2026-08-31 (after a 2020-2026 gap); pydivsufsort 0.0.20 released 2025-12-12; 5 open issues, newest 2026-10-20. Issue response time not assessed.
FMIndex: Contains/FindFirst/Count/Locate, GetSnippet, RestoreSourceText; SuffixArray.Search; text kept as Text. Hard cap: Create() throws above 100,000,000 chars, so not genome-size.
First-class wildcards: SuffixArray.SearchWildcard (*,? with min/max length, stop chars), FMIndex.LocateWildcard/LocateSingleGapped/LocateMultiGapped. No IUPAC codes or character classes.
FMIndex.LocateFuzzy: edit distance (sub/ins/del; flags disable ins/del for mismatch-only) by recursive backward search. XML docs warn of blow-up; no search schemes or pruning bounds.
SuffixArray.SearchCommon/SearchLongestCommon(text1,text2,minLength) list common substrings with positions in both texts; SearchRepeated for self-repeats. Not MEM/MUM semantics; 100M-char cap.
No matching-statistics or streaming-anchor API in the public surface (SuffixArray, LcpIndex, FMIndex member lists).
Only pairwise two-text static methods (SearchCommon/SearchLongestCommon with text1,text2). No generalized index over k texts, no document listing or counting.
No reverse-complement or strand-aware search; text is UTF-16 chars only. User would append the reverse complement themselves.
Exposes SA, LCP and Rank arrays (ReadOnlyMemory<int>) and LcpIndex.GetLcp with O(1) RMQ. No node, suffix-link, parent/child or LCA API.
LcpIndex.CountUniqueSubstrings, FindRepeats, FindTandemRepeats, CalculateZivLempelComplexity; SuffixArray.SearchLongestRepeated/SearchRepeated. No supermaximal repeats.
SA-IS O(N) plus Kasai LCP in managed C#; README publishes no build times. Usable up to the 100M-char cap (benchmarked on 100 MB DNA). Native libsais likely faster by a clear margin.
SuffixArray holds int[] SA + LCP + Rank + UTF-16 text (about 14 B/char by source reading, not measured). FM sampling-32 serialized is 17.25 MB for the 100 MB DNA file; RAM size unpublished.
Published (Snapdragon X Plus, .NET 9, BenchmarkDotNet, dna.50MB): FMIndex.Count 493-728 ns per 7-16-mer, 27 ns single char. No head-to-head vs native FM-indexes (likely 2-3x slower).
Documented hard limit: Create() throws ArgumentOutOfRangeException above 100,000,000 chars; positions are int. Human-scale text needs redesign.
Entirely in-memory; Deserialize loads the whole structure. No mmap or semi-external build/query.
No parallel construction: no Parallel, thread or lock usage found in the SuffixArray, FMIndex, LcpIndex or BurrowsWheelerTransform sources.
No thread-safety statement and no lock or Interlocked in the sources; query methods look read-only. Concurrent use is neither documented nor tested.
Static indexes only: Create() from a complete text; no append, insert or delete.
FMIndex with sampling-32: serialized 17.25 MB vs SuffixArray 417.5 MB on the 100 MB DNA file (about 24x smaller); wavelet-matrix BWT. Not run-length or pangenome scale.
Text is .NET string / ReadOnlyMemory<char> (any UTF-16 symbols; wavelet matrix adapts to small alphabets). No integer-alphabet text index and no 2-bit DNA path.
Serialize/Deserialize to byte[], file or Stream, Brotli-compressed with XxHash32 checksum. No mmap load, no format spec or version field found.
Native .NET 8/9/10 API using Span/ReadOnlySpan/ReadOnlyMemory, records for matches, XML docs with documented exceptions. Text type is char-only (no generic alphabet).
NuGet package (net8-10, netstandard2.1) plus a DocFX site. No CLI or server/MCP surface.
MSTest unit tests per class in tests/ (SuffixArrayTests, FMIndexTests, LcpIndexTests ...). No CI workflow found and no oracle or fuzz comparison seen.
MIT; 6 releases 2025-10-13 to 2025-11-16 (latest 11.5 months old); 11 commits, 2 stars, 1 open PR. Little issue activity, single maintainer.

bwa fastmap prints SMEMs with hit counts and positions (-w caps interval size for locate); bowtie2-inspect dumps indexed sequences. No contains/count API apart from C functions bwt_match_exact, bwt_sa.
Only ambiguity handling: Bowtie2 --np penalty for N in read or reference, --n-ceil; BWA turns N into a random base in .pac. No IUPAC, wildcards or classes in queries.
bwa aln: bounded edit distance -n (INT or FLOAT), gap opens -o, extensions -e (-1 = k-difference), seed edits -k. Bowtie2 -N seed mismatches + DP extension. CLI-level, no library call.
bwa fastmap reports super-maximal exact matches (SMEMs) with min length -l. Not the full MEM set between two texts and no MUM filter; BWA-MEM uses MEM seeds internally.
Public C API bwt_smem1/bwt_smem1a returns SMEMs along a query (bidirectional BWT, Li 2013); fastmap prints them. Equivalent to matching-statistics anchors, but no ms[] array and sparse docs.
Multi-FASTA indexed as one concatenation with .ann/.amb contig tables; hits mapped to contig+offset (README FAQ 5). No k-common, LCS or document-listing API.
bwa index packs forward + reverse complement into the BWT (bntseq.c: 'add the reverse complemented sequence'); Bowtie2 aligns read and revcomp to one index (--nofw/--norc). Strand-aware coordinates.
FM-index only: public C functions bwt_extend (bidirectional interval extension), bwt_occ, bwt_sa act on SA intervals. No tree, suffix-link, parent/child or LCA API; undocumented.
No analytics (LRS, distinct substrings, k-mer statistics) in either tool; bowtie2-inspect only lists names or a summary of the index.
No bp/s published. BWA: IS algorithm (<2 GB) or BWT-SW blockwise (-a bwtsw) for large genomes. Bowtie2: blockwise, optional libsais + OpenMP since 2.5.3 ('significant speed-up').
Bowtie2 manual: human-genome FM index about 3.2 GB RAM (~1 B/char). Li & Durbin 2009: BWA ~2.3 GB for 3 Gb (n bytes for genomes <4 Gb). SA sampling tunable (--offrate); smaller compressed FMs exist.
No exact-query latency published, only read-mapper throughput. Class: FM backward search O(m) with occ checkpoints; Bowtie2 -p scaling 'close to linear'. Not head-to-head with other indexes.

Bowtie2 manual: indexes genomes of any size, 64-bit 'large' .bt2l index above ~4 Gbp. BWA FAQ: works on references >4 GB total since 0.6.x (each chromosome <2 GB); human genome is the standard use case.
Bowtie2 --mm memory-maps the index (shared across processes); bowtie2-build blockwise (--bmax/--dcv) trades time for RAM; BWA bwtsw -b block size. Neither is truly disk-resident build + query.
bowtie2-build --threads (default 1; speeds up 'considerably in most cases'; libsais route needs OpenMP). bwa index is single-threaded. No near-linear speed-up figure published.
bowtie2 -p and bwa mem -t share one read-only index across threads (Bowtie2: 'speedup is close to linear'); --mm shares one image across processes; bwa.h has bwa_idx_load_from_shm.
Static indexes; no append, insert or delete. Any change requires rebuilding with bowtie2-build or bwa index.
FM-index with sampled SA: Bowtie2 human index ~3.2 GB; BWA ~2.3 GB vs ~12 GB for a plain human SA (Li & Durbin 2009), about 5x smaller. Not run-length or pangenome scale.
DNA only: 2-bit packed ACGT (.pac/.bwt; BWA bwt_t 'about seq_len/4' bytes); N mapped to a random base or penalised. No general or integer alphabets; DNA optimisation is the design core.
Documented index file sets (.amb .ann .bwt .pac .sa; .1-.4/.rev.1-.2 .bt2/.bt2l); Bowtie2 --mm memory-mapped load. No checksum or format-version guarantee documented.
BWA exposes a C API (bwa.h/bwt.h: bwa_idx_build/load, bwt_smem1, bwt_extend; extern C) usable via P/Invoke, unversioned and thinly documented. Bowtie2 is C++/CLI only.
Bioconda (conda, pixi, BioContainers docker): bwa 0.7.19-1 and bowtie2 2.5.5-2; GitHub release tarballs; BWA also on SourceForge; CLI-first tools. No NuGet or MCP surface.
Bowtie2 CI (simple-tests, random-tests workflows) runs make simple-test/random-test on Linux and macOS, with and without AVX2. BWA CI only compiles (gcc/clang, aarch64). Test scripts not read.
